newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe tobacco industry urges renewal of Lome.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe tobacco industry urges renewal of Lome.

text.p: Zimbabwe's key export tobacco industry on Wednesday urged the government to persist in negotiations to secure the renewal or extension of the Lome Convention which ensures preferential entry of its commodities into European markets.

Top officials from the Zimbabwe Tobacco Association (ZTA) and Tobacco Traders Association (TTA) warned that the non-renewal of the convention would seriously erode the price competitiveness of Zimbabwe's tobacco crop in Europe.

"Forty-six percent of Zimbabwean tobacco is exported to countries in the European Union (EU) which represents the greatest proportion of this country's exports to that area," ZTA president Robert Webb told a ZTA annual congress.

"The review of the Lome Convention trade agreement, which presently gives us partial duty free status, expires in the year 2000. This will seriously threaten our price competitiveness. We urge government to continue negotiations now to ensure our security of trade in this area," he said.
The Lome Convention is a trade agreement between the European Union and African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states giving ACP commodities preferential entry into the EU.

TTA president Jim van Heerden said the background against which the convention was being reviewed did not favour renewal with the new World Trade Organisation (WTO) seeking to enforce reciprocal trading relations to which the EU should conform with.

"In addition, many ACP states have not taken full advantage of Lome to improve their economic and trade relations with Europe and new geopolitical conditions within Europe itself have served to refocus attention on the value of aid and trade-related tariff preferences," he said.
Van Heerden said Zimbabwe, the world's second largest exporter of flue-cured tobacco after Brazil, needed to make a good case for renewal or extension of the convention.

Earlier, Webb urged growers to raise output of the yellow leaf by 14 percent to 245 million kgs in 1998 to ensure the country's stay in the top league despite what he described as the industry's war against a minefield of controls and regulations.

He said the tobacco industry, locally and abroad, was going through a period of violent change and upheaval with costly litigations and lawsuits in the United States and violent anti- smoking lobbies worldwide.

"Coupled with the ripple effect of these pressures, the producer here in Zimbabwe is faced with punitive taxes on an export crop, excessive interest rates, rising costs of production often in excess of government's consumer price index and diversion of monies raised by growers," he said.
Webb said the government's 10 percent levy introduced last year on tobacco sales -- five percent payable by growers and the other five by traders -- was unsustainable.

The industry has for the past year been lobbying President Robert Mugabe's cash-strapped government, which says it needs to boost its coffers to fund essential public projects, to scrap the levy which it regards as punitive double taxation. REUTER ES SM
